title: Taste & Craft: A Conversation with Tuomas Artman, CTO Linear & Gergely Orosz, @pragmaticengineer

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is primarily about product design quality, human taste in engineering, and how humans must maintain deliberate product judgment when AI accelerates shipping speed.

summary: Tuomas Artman and Gergely Orosz explore how AI agents risk swinging shipping speed too far without thoughtful product design. Artman argues engineering difficulty was a natural gate forcing deliberation, but AI removes that friction. Linear combats this by grouping customer feedback to find root problems rather than shipping requests as-is. AI helps accelerate bug fixing—roughly 10% of bugs auto-fixed with PRs and no engineer involvement. On Claude Code, Artman notes visible quality bugs from competitive pressure to ship fast. Drawing on shared Uber experience, they discuss how revenue and golden metrics made quality unmeasurable. Artman's thesis: when products converge on features and price, users migrate to higher-quality options, making quality a durable moat. Linear's Quality Wednesdays originated when Artman found 35 problems in a tiny UI menu during an offsite. Engineers must independently find quality fixes weekly, creating constant quality awareness and fewer regressions. Linear has fixed 2,500-3,000 small quality details to date. The zero bug policy auto-assigns bugs immediately as highest priority, fixed within 7 days (usually 2-3 hours), after an initial 3-week feature freeze. Artman argues fixing bugs immediately costs the same effort as fixing them months later. On AI and taste, agents lack time perception and can't feel frustration from slow interactions. A design engineer's experiment showed agents could build animations but produced unnatural ease-in timing. Linear builds its quality-focused engineering culture through deliberate hiring: a rigorous process including a full-week paid trial where candidates implement a greenfield project, sometimes even shipping it. This yields very few hiring misses compared to traditional multi-interview processes. All engineers have access to Slack channels with big customers, and every customer meeting is recorded and tagged so anyone can search customer feedback. Artman predicts all software engineers will become product engineers as AI commoditizes implementation work—engineers who merely pipe data between systems won't be needed, but those who understand customer needs and good UX will. Closing advice for aspiring product engineers: get hands-on with customers, build things yourself, and read Apple's Human Interface Guidelines for UX foundations.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The danger of shipping features too quickly with AI
sections.summary: Artman warns that AI agents make it too easy to ship every feature request immediately, risking convoluted software and poor UX. He cites Steve Jobs's principle of saying no to 999 things. Engineering difficulty used to be a natural gate forcing thoughtful design before building.

sections.title: Hypergrowth parallels and competitive pressure
sections.summary: Orosz challenges whether this problem predates AI. Artman draws parallels to Uber's hypergrowth, where winner-takes-all pressure led to shipping at all costs. With AI, competition includes small teams or individuals who can match feature sets, making tasteful, high-quality software a competitive differentiator.

sections.title: How Linear approaches feature requests and development
sections.summary: Linear still thinks deliberately about every feature, never shipping prototypes or customer requests as-is. They gather feedback, group it to find root causes, and design complete UX solutions. AI accelerates bug fixing—10% of bugs now auto-fixed with PRs and no engineer—but feature design still requires human time and taste.

sections.title: Thoughts on Anthropic's Claude Code
sections.summary: Artman notes Claude Code was itself coded by Claude, and visible bugs and quality issues are immediately apparent when using it. He attributes this to Anthropic's competitive pressure against OpenAI, making it a live example of the speed-over-quality tradeoff under discussion.

sections.title: The challenge of measuring software quality
sections.summary: Artman and Orosz discuss how Uber's golden metrics (especially revenue) made quality effectively unmeasurable. Artman recalls an early Uber engineer who measured a two-pixel offset in code review, showing initial quality culture that eroded as scaling incentives dominated. His thesis: when products converge on price and features, users eventually choose the higher-quality option, making quality a long-term moat.

sections.title: Quality Wednesdays at Linear
sections.summary: Artman explains the origin of Quality Wednesdays: frustrated by repeatedly pointing out small quality details like 150ms fade-out highlights, he brought the team together at an offsite to find problems in a small UI view. They found 35 issues in a tiny menu, revealing the product had thousands of similar small defects. To date, Linear has fixed 2,500-3,000 such details. Every Wednesday, engineers must independently find and present a quality fix. The side effect is constant quality awareness—engineers introduce fewer regressions because they're always on the lookout.

sections.title: The zero bug policy explained
sections.summary: Artman explains that zero bug policy means every reported bug is auto-assigned immediately as the engineer's highest priority. Bugs are fixed within 7 days, usually 2-3 hours. The rationale: bug creation rate is constant, so fixing immediately costs the same total effort as fixing months later. Linear froze new feature work for 3 weeks to clear the backlog to zero, then maintained the policy. Bug fixes don't count for Quality Wednesday—those require independent quality improvements. Artman believes every company should adopt zero bug policy, especially now that AI helps identify and fix bugs.

sections.title: AI agents and the lack of human taste in design
sections.summary: Artman explains why quality and AI agents rarely appear in the same sentence: AI lacks taste. Agents have no concept of time—they can't get frustrated when a click takes 2 seconds. A design engineer's experiment showed agents could build animations but produced unnatural ease-in timing; manual refinement made them feel natural. The last bastion for AI is tasteful, purpose-built UI with great design and the ability to understand what users feel.

sections.title: Building a culture of product-focused engineering
sections.summary: Artman explains Linear's hiring and culture practices. They hire specifically for product engineers who want to build beautiful, high-quality software. A key component is a full-week paid trial where candidates implement a greenfield project, sometimes even shipping it. This rigorous process yields very few hiring misses compared to traditional multi-interview approaches at Uber. Once hired, engineers are immersed in customer feedback: Slack channels with big customers are open to all, and every customer meeting is recorded and tagged so anyone can search what customers want. This creates an inescapable fire hose of customer pain and joy.

sections.title: The future role of software engineers as product engineers
sections.summary: Artman predicts all engineers will become product engineers as AI commoditizes implementation. Four years ago AI couldn't write code; now it commands codebases. Four years ahead, if exponential growth continues, engineers who merely pipe data between systems won't be needed, but those who understand customer needs and good UX will. Engineers must become mini-PMs who engage with customers and then implement what customers want. Orosz notes the accumulating role expansion: from one language to multiple, then QA, DevOps, and now PM and customer support responsibilities.

sections.title: Closing advice for aspiring product engineers
sections.summary: Artman's closing advice for engineers wanting to develop product sense: get closer to customers, build things yourself to learn hands-on, ship to the world to get real user feedback, and read Apple's Human Interface Guidelines as the best UX resource. The two biggest things are direct customer engagement and building independently.
